blocks.prompt: The Bread That Was Alive
blocks.text: Yeast is alive. It is so small that you need a microscope to see it. A spoonful of yeast holds billions of them. When you mix yeast into dough, the yeast starts to eat. It eats sugar from the flour. Then it burps out a gas. The gas is called carbon dioxide. It is the same gas you breathe out. The gas makes bubbles. The bubbles get stuck in the stretchy dough. Slowly, the dough puffs up like a balloon. In the hot oven, the bubbles grow bigger. Then the dough sets hard around them. Cut the loaf open and you can see every bubble the yeast made.

3.title: The Bread That Was Alive
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: The Tiny Bakers
blocks.text: Bread is made from four things: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Three of them are not alive. The fourth one is. Yeast is a fungus, a tiny cousin of mushrooms, but each yeast is a single cell, far too small to see without a microscope. When you stir yeast into warm dough, you are feeding a huge crowd of living things. The yeast finds sugar in the flour and eats it. Like anything that eats, it makes waste. Yeast waste is a gas called carbon dioxide, the same gas that leaves your mouth when you breathe out. The gas has nowhere to go. Flour and water make a stretchy web inside the dough, and the bubbles get caught in it. Millions of bubbles push outward at once, and the dough swells. The oven finishes the job. Heat makes every bubble grow, the dough stretches one last time, and then it turns firm and holds that shape. The yeast dies in the heat. So every hole in a slice of bread is a room the yeast built.

4.title: The Bread That Was Alive
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Flour holds two proteins: glutenin and gliadin
Wet them and knead, and they link into gluten
Gluten is the stretchy web that traps the gas
Oven spring: the last fast rise in the heat
The Maillard reaction browns the crust

blocks.prompt: Why Bread Has Holes
blocks.text: Pick up a slice of bread and hold it to the light. It is full of holes. The holes are not a mistake. They are the whole point, and something alive put them there. Bread begins as flour, water, salt, and yeast. Yeast is a fungus, and each grain of it is a single living cell. Give it warmth, water, and sugar and it does what living things do. It eats, and it makes waste. Yeast waste comes out as carbon dioxide, the same gas you exhale. The gas cannot escape, because flour is more than powder. It carries two proteins, glutenin and gliadin. Dry, they do nothing at all. Add water and knead the dough, and they link into gluten, a stretchy web running through the whole lump. Every bubble of yeast gas gets trapped in that web, and as millions of bubbles inflate, the dough rises. Then comes the oven and one last surge that bakers call oven spring. The trapped gas expands in the heat, the loaf swells fast, and for a moment the dough is stretched as far as it will go. Near 140 degrees Fahrenheit the yeast dies. The starch drinks up water and stiffens, the gluten sets, and the shape locks in place for good. The crust is a separate piece of chemistry. Where the surface gets dry and hot, sugars and proteins react with one another and build hundreds of new flavor compounds. That reaction has a name, the Maillard reaction, and it is the reason toast smells like toast while raw dough smells like almost nothing. So a loaf is a kind of record. Every hole is a room a yeast cell built and then died inside.

5.title: The Bread That Was Alive
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Bread is older than farming

blocks.prompt: Fourteen Thousand Years of Bubbles
blocks.text: For a long time the story went like this: people learned to farm, farming gave them grain, and grain gave them bread. Then archaeologists working at a site called Shubayqa 1, in the desert of northeastern Jordan, sifted through an ancient fireplace and found burnt crumbs. Under a microscope the crumbs turned out to be flatbread, ground from wild grain and wild tubers, baked on hot stones about 14,400 years ago. The people who made it were hunters and gatherers. Nobody farmed anything for another four thousand years. The story had been running backward. Bread did not come from farming. Bread may be part of why people bothered to farm at all. Those first flatbreads were flat because nothing in them made gas. Leavened bread, the puffed kind, was almost certainly an accident. Yeast drifts through the air and settles on grain, on skin, on everything. Leave a bowl of wet flour alone in a warm room and wild yeast finds it, feeds on the sugars, and fills the mush with carbon dioxide. Someone, somewhere, baked a bowl of forgotten batter instead of throwing it out, and it came out light. A sourdough starter is that same accident, kept alive on purpose. It is a small ecosystem in a jar: wild yeast making gas, and lactic acid bacteria making acid. The acid is what gives sourdough its tang and what keeps most spoiling microbes out. Bakers have kept some starters going for decades, feeding them flour like a pet. Bread pushed its way into language, too. A companion is literally someone you share bread with, from the Latin words for with and bread. The English word lord began as hlafweard, the loaf keeper, and lady began as the loaf kneader. That is how central this stuff was. The person with the bread was the person in charge. We treat a loaf as ordinary. It is one of the oldest technologies we still use every single day, and it is run by a fungus we cannot see.

6.title: The Bread That Was Alive
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Saccharomyces cerevisiae: baker's yeast, brewer's yeast, one species
Fermentation makes carbon dioxide and alcohol; the alcohol bakes off
Yeast inflates air pockets made by mixing, it cannot start a bubble
Gluten: glutenin for strength, gliadin for stretch
Maillard reaction: sugars plus amino acids equals crust flavor
Carbonized loaves survive from Pompeii, AD 79, scored and stamped

blocks.prompt: A Loaf Is a Fossil of Its Own Making
blocks.text: Bread looks like the simplest food on the table, and it is one of the most complicated things most people make. Four ingredients, one of them alive, and a set of reactions that a chemist would be pleased to have designed on purpose. Start with the flour, which is mostly starch plus about ten percent protein. Two of those proteins matter: glutenin, which is strong and springy, and gliadin, which is loose and flowing. Dry, they sit in the sack and do nothing. Add water and work the dough, and they bond into long tangled chains called gluten. Glutenin gives that network its strength, gliadin lets it flow and stretch, and between them they make a fabric that can hold a gas without tearing. This is why kneading matters. You are not mixing. You are building a structure. Now the living part. Baker's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a single-celled fungus, and it is the same species brewers use to make beer. In the dough it finds sugars, some already present and some released as enzymes cut the starch apart, and it ferments them. Fermentation yields two products: carbon dioxide and alcohol. The alcohol boils away in the oven. The gas stays, and the gas is the whole show. Here is the detail almost everyone gets wrong. Yeast cannot create a bubble. Carbon dioxide dissolves into the water of the dough first, and it can only come out of solution into a gas pocket that already exists. Those pockets come from you, whisked in during mixing and kneading. The yeast does not build the holes. It inflates the ones you gave it. A loaf that was mixed carelessly has fewer places for gas to gather, and it bakes up coarse and uneven. Then the oven, where four things happen at once and in order. The trapped gas expands with heat and the loaf leaps upward in a final rise bakers call oven spring. Near 140 degrees Fahrenheit the yeast dies, its work finished. The starch granules absorb water and swell into a solid gel while the gluten proteins tighten and set, converting a stretchy bag of gas into a firm sponge that will keep its shape. Last, at the surface, where the crust has dried out and climbed past 300 degrees, sugars and amino acids collide in the Maillard reaction and generate hundreds of new aromatic compounds. Toast smells like toast for this reason. Raw dough smells like almost nothing at all. What is left when it cools is a fossil. Not a fossil of some other creature, but a cast of the loaf's own history: every hole a bubble, every bubble a place where a fungus exhaled, every wall a protein that stretched and then froze. We have been doing this a long time. Carbonized loaves pulled from the ovens of Pompeii, buried in AD 79, are scored into neat wedges and pressed with a stamp bearing the baker's name, so a Roman could tell whose bread was whose. That baker understood almost none of the chemistry above. He did not need to. The yeast did the work, and the loaf kept the record.
